newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spanish markets expect fiscal discipline for 1998.
newsitem.headline: Spanish markets expect fiscal discipline for 1998.

text.p: Spanish debt is likely to take in its stride an initial review on Friday of the 1998 budget, confident it will exhibit fiscal discipline and strengthen the nation's bid to join Europe's single currency launch.

Economy Minister Rodrigo Rato plans to present the guiding framework of the 1998 budget to a regular news conference on Friday following the weekly cabinet meeting. The draft must be presented to the legislature by the end of September.

"This will be a budget that shows the same rigour that we have had this year. But I doubt there will be a rally because the news won't be very new. Some of the numbers have been filtered," said Valentin Fernandez, economist at Credit Lyonnais in Madrid.

Since mid-July, Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar and Rato have revealed that growth for 1998 is expected to be 3.4 percent with inflation at 2.1 percent. The 1998 deficit objective is 2.4 percent of GDP from a projected 3.0 in 1997.
Although economists call these underlying assumptions optimistic, they add that they are possible and should serve to underpin the Spanish market.
There is, too, little room for the market to outpace based on domestic fundamentals since it has soared in recent weeks.
The Spanish 10-year bond spread to its German counterpart -- a measure of the added risk of holding Spanish debt -- remains near an all-time low of 59 basis points, set on July 28.
In March of 1996, this spread stood at 330 basis points, and at more than 500 in the summer of 1995.
"The framework for the 1998 budget looks very encouraging, but whether it will push the market to new highs is very debatable," said Craig Shute, fixed-income analyst at Bear Stearns in London.
Henrik Lumholdt, economist at Bank of America, said the spread would likely remain little changed on the news, although the budget will help underpin the market.
Given funding costs and credit risks, the minimum spread possible is around 40 basis points, he said, but that would mean assigning a 100 percent chance to Spain entering EMU on time.
This is difficult when there are worries about the entire project being delayed, analysts said.
Still, the budget is the firmest evidence Spain can provide to doubting northern neighbours that it has indeed converted a nation of once lax financing into a bastion of fiscal probity.
"It is going to be good for Spain with regard to European economic and monetary union. It will show Spain consolidating budgetary rigour and that this year isn't a one-off," he said.

Spain, in the space of just one year and from humble economic circumstances, has managed to whip its economy into shape. In just one year, the conservative government met single currency requirements on foreign exchange, long-term rates and inflation and is well on the way to hitting the deficit target tied to the key 1997 budget of three percent of GDP.
Debt will be too high, but will be declining.
"It's probably going to be a budget that will once again consolidate its EMU changes," Shute said.
